<reason>Both sides were disciplined and rhetorically strong, but B controlled the decisive clash. B reframed the conceded cost early (bands are ranges; level placement, bonuses, and off-cycle tools survive; only unexplained deviation disappears) and then won nearly every major exchange: "a confession of what—deviating from the structure the firm itself wrote," the point that market signals reach only the already-mobile, and the catch that stalling promotions lowers the very rate being published, which forced A into an explicit concession ("True, and beside the point"). Most decisively, B's Q1 exposed the circularity in A's targeted-enforcement alternative—discovery needs a claim, a claim needs suspicion, suspicion needs a fact secrecy hides—and A's A1 answer ("a worker who suspects can file a charge") presupposed exactly the suspicion at issue. B crystallized this in the closing; A never repaired it. A landed real hits (public-sector category error, the worker-mobility reframe, the firm-wide-rewrite timing point), but B absorbed them with headroom/off-cycle tools and the irony that A's counteroffer scenario itself runs on transparency elsewhere. Grounding was clean on both sides—B's Ledbetter and Colorado/New York references were hedged, ordinary background knowledge, not fake precision. B simply left more of A's case answered than vice versa.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: the self-defeat point on gaming ("you cannot game a promotion metric upward by promoting less") forced A's concession, and the unanswered circularity answer to A's "targeted enforcement" alternative (claim needs suspicion, suspicion needs a fact secrecy hides) became the debate's decisive, unrepaired burden.</best_rebuttal>
